Let me analyze this task. I need to estimate the software development effort for implementing a software increment described in the specification, which contains 8 user stories (U1-U8) related to Hyperledger Fabric.

Let me break down each user story:

**U1: Capabilities Framework** - This is a big one. Implementing the capabilities framework in Hyperledger Fabric:
- Add capabilities maps to channel config (channel level, application level, orderer level)
- Define capability strings (V1.1) in fabric/common/capabilities/
- Modify channelconfig API (api.go) to define capability interfaces
- Orderer must support orderer + channel capabilities, peer must support application + channel capabilities
- Crash behavior when capabilities not supported
- Enforcement that orderer capabilities are turned on before application group can enable them
- This is substantial work

**U2: Read-Your-Writes (RYW) during key retrieval** - Extend chaincode API with `stub.GetTrxState(key string)`:
- Modify chaincode shim API
- Implement transaction-scoped state access (read from write set first)
- Testing

**U3: Video tutorial for adding organizations to a running network**:
- Create a video with a diagram (ppt-style image)
- Go through the process of adding orgs without bringing down the network
- This is a documentation/training deliverable, not strictly code

**U4: Performance testing of Fabric queries with CouchDB**:
- Set up performance tests for queries with CouchDB as state database
- Measure and report performance

**U5: Construct channel config block outside configtxgen**:
- Make MSPConfig an interface (or similar refactoring) to allow constructing own configs programmatically
- Refactor configtx library to be usable as a library

**U6: Remove chaincode singletons**:
- Refactor chaincode support to remove singletons (prerequisite for lifecycle work)
- Makes development and testing easier

**U7: Test setup generating peer core.yaml and orderer.yaml from World config**:
- Test infrastructure work - generate config files based on values in a "World" config (sounds like a BDD/cucumber-style test framework)

**U8: New lifecycle validation parameters interface**:
- Implement interface returning validation parameters for a chaincode
- Special edge case: return validation info for '_lifecycle' itself with auto-generated signature policy requiring majority of orgs to endorse

I could structure activities per user story, with sub-activities like design, implementation, unit testing, integration testing, documentation, review, etc.

technical_and_design_decisions: All code changes are implemented in Go within the existing Hyperledger Fabric code base (peer, orderer, common/channelconfig, common/capabilities, chaincode shim, configtx), following existing Fabric architecture and coding conventions.

U1: Capabilities are modeled as three independent string-keyed maps in channel config: /Channel (both orderer and peer must support), /Channel/Orderer (orderer only), and /Channel/Application (peer only).
U1: Only a single capability flag "V1.1" is introduced in each of the three maps; no finer-grained capabilities are added in this increment, and V1.2 is treated as a future superset.
U1: Fail-fast semantics: a binary that does not support a required capability crashes on processing the channel config, rather than attempting graceful degradation.

U1: Capability gating is exposed to consumers through semantic boolean methods on ChannelCapabilities/OrdererCapabilities/ApplicationCapabilities interfaces (in common/channelconfig/api.go), so consuming code never performs version string logic.

U1: The orderer enforces that orderer-level capabilities are enabled before an application group is allowed to enable application capabilities, preventing a blockchain fork during the initial v1.0->v1.1 upgrade.
U2: Read-your-writes is exposed via a new shim method stub.GetTrxState(key); reads first consult the current transaction's write set (tx simulation results) before falling back to the state database.
U3: The deliverable is a recorded screencast video (MP4) plus one architecture/flow diagram slide; the procedure is first executed and validated hands-on against a live multi-org network.
U4: Query performance is measured with a benchmark driver against a network using CouchDB as state database, covering rich queries and pagination, with results published as a written report.

U5: configtx internals are refactored so MSP configuration is handled through interfaces, exposing a reusable library API that lets developers construct a channel config block programmatically without invoking the configtxgen binary.
U6: Chaincode support singletons are removed via constructor-based dependency injection wired from the peer startup path.
U7: The test framework generates peer core.yaml and orderer.yaml from a central World configuration object instead of shipping static YAML files.

U8: The new lifecycle implements the validation-parameters interface; the special '_lifecycle' chaincode returns an automatically generated signature policy requiring endorsement by a majority of channel organizations.
assumptions: A single experienced Go developer, already familiar with the Hyperledger Fabric code base, personally performs all work; estimates are pure effort (work-hours), not elapsed calendar time.

Estimates cover design, implementation, unit/integration testing, documentation, and code-review rework, but exclude waiting time for external reviewers, CI queue time, and project management overhead.
A working Fabric build/test environment, CI infrastructure, benchmark hardware, and video-recording tools are already available; no time is included for procuring or installing tooling.
For U1, the referenced Gerrit changes serve as design guidance only; the full framework (schema, APIs, orderer/peer integration, tooling, tests) is implemented in this increment.
For U2, scope is limited to single-key retrieval of transaction-updated values; range/rich queries over uncommitted writes are out of scope.
For U3, the developer performs the video production personally; effort for the video is counted as development work for the increment.
For U4, existing performance-test harnesses can be extended; building a brand-new benchmarking framework from scratch is not required.
For U8, the new lifecycle code base from the companion task exists; only the validation-parameters interface and its integration are estimated here.
Breaking-change documentation for the mutual-TLS-style 'stops working' class of changes (linked to FAB-6000) is out of scope; only the capabilities framework (FAB-5999 class) is included.
No additional capabilities beyond "V1.1" are required in this increment, and no graceful (non-crash) unsupported-capability handling is required.

activities.activity_description: Analyze the requirements, review referenced Gerrit changes and design doc, and produce the detailed design: three capability maps in channel config, V1.1 flag, crash semantics, and upgrade flow.

activities.activity_name: U1 - Channel config schema and parsing for capabilities maps
activities.activity_description: Extend the channel config protobuf/schema and configtx parsing to carry the channel-, orderer-, and application-level capabilities maps, including validation of the new config value.
Implement common/capabilities packages (channel.go, orderer.go, application.go) with the capability registry, supported-capability lists, and the V1.1 capability constant.

Define and implement ChannelCapabilities, OrdererCapabilities, and ApplicationCapabilities interfaces in common/channelconfig/api.go and their implementations, mapping capability strings to semantic boolean methods.

Integrate capability checks into the orderer: crash on unsupported channel/orderer capabilities, and enforce that orderer capabilities are enabled before application capabilities can be enabled (fork prevention on initial upgrade).
Integrate capability checks into the peer so it crashes on unsupported channel/application capabilities when processing channel configuration (join and reconfiguration commits).
Update configtxgen, configtxlator, and sample config profiles so channels can be created and reconfigured with the V1.1 capability in each of the three maps.
Write unit tests for capability providers, channelconfig APIs, config parsing, and the orderer fork-prevention rule.

Build integration tests for the rolling-upgrade scenario: network operates during binary upgrade, reconfiguration enables V1.1, rogue v1.0 peer crashes, and premature application-capability enablement is rejected.
Document how to gate a non-backwards-compatible change behind a capability (steps 1-4 of the spec) and the operational upgrade procedure.
Design the read-your-writes semantics and shim API extension (stub.GetTrxState), including interaction with the transaction read/write set.
Implement GetTrxState in the chaincode shim and the corresponding handler/protocol support between shim and peer.
Implement peer-side support so the query resolves keys already written in the active transaction before consulting the state database.
Unit tests and an end-to-end chaincode test demonstrating access to keys written earlier in the same transaction.
Update shim API documentation and a sample chaincode snippet showing GetTrxState usage.

Hands-on execution and scripting of the full procedure for adding a new organization to a running network (config update, signing, channel update) without downtime, to ensure the video content is correct.
Create the introductory slide/diagram illustrating what happens when an organization is added to a live network.
Record the narrated walkthrough of the procedure, edit the footage, and produce the final video.
Review the video for technical accuracy, add supporting notes/commands, and publish the deliverable.
Define the query workload (rich queries, range queries, pagination), data volumes, and metrics for CouchDB-backed query performance evaluation.
Provision a Fabric network configured with CouchDB as the state database and load it with benchmark data.
Implement or extend performance test drivers issuing the defined query workloads and collecting latency/throughput metrics.
Run the benchmarks, collect results, and analyze query performance characteristics with CouchDB.
Write and publish the performance report with findings and recommendations for network managers.
Design the interface-based MSP configuration handling and the public API surface for constructing channel config blocks in code.
Refactor configtx/configtxgen internals into a reusable library, making MSP config construction interface-based so custom configs can be built programmatically.
Unit tests for the new library API plus an example program that builds a channel config block without invoking configtxgen.
Document the new library API and migration notes for existing configtxgen users.

activities.activity_name: U6 - Singleton inventory and refactoring design
activities.activity_description: Inventory all chaincode-related singletons and design the dependency-injection structure to replace them.
Refactor the chaincode support package(s) to remove singletons, introducing constructor-injected dependencies throughout.

activities.activity_name: U6 - Peer wiring and test repair
activities.activity_description: Update peer startup wiring for the injected dependencies and repair/refactor all affected unit tests.
Design the mapping from the test framework's World configuration to generated peer core.yaml and orderer.yaml files.
Implement the generator that produces core.yaml and orderer.yaml from World config values within the test framework.
Integrate the generator into existing test scenarios and validate that generated configs drive peers/orderers correctly.
Design the interface returning validation parameters (endorsement policy and related info) for a chaincode in the new lifecycle.
Implement the interface in the new lifecycle, including the '_lifecycle' edge case returning an automatically generated signature policy requiring majority-of-orgs endorsement.
Unit tests covering normal chaincodes and the '_lifecycle' special case edge conditions.
Integrate the new validation-parameters source into the peer commit/VSCC validation path and verify end-to-end behavior.
Final cross-feature integration, full regression test run across all eight user stories, defect fixing, and release notes for the software increment.
